'''''Hard Eight''''' (originally titled '''''Sydney''''')<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-09-10|title=Paul Thomas Anderson's 'Hard Eight', AKA 'Sydney': "It's Always Good to Meet a New Friend" • Cinephilia & Beyond|url=https://cinephiliabeyond.org/hard-eight-aka-sydney/|access-date=2020-09-19|website=Cinephilia & Beyond|language=en-US|archive-date=2020-09-21|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921144356/https://cinephiliabeyond.org/hard-eight-aka-sydney/|url-status=live}}</ref> is a 1996 American [[crime film]] written and directed by [[Paul Thomas Anderson]] in his feature directorial debut, and starring [[Philip Baker Hall]], [[John C. Reilly]], [[Gwyneth Paltrow]], and [[Samuel L. Jackson]]. An expansion on Anderson's 1993 short film ''[[Cigarettes & Coffee]]'', it follows the bond between a senior gambler and a homeless man. It premiered at the 1996 [[Sundance Film Festival]].<ref>Conrad, Mark T. ''The Philosophy of Neo-Noir'', 2009. [[The University Press of Kentucky]]. {{ISBN|081319217X}}.</ref>

The film's title refers to a "hard eight," a wager in the casino game of [[craps]] that the shooter will roll two fours before a seven or any other combination totaling eight.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Nayman |first1=Adam |title=Paul Thomas Anderson: Masterworks |date=2020 |publisher=Abrams Books |page=135 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Paul_Thomas_Anderson_Masterworks/To7QDwAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=hard+eight+bet+craps+scene&pg=PA135&printsec=frontcover |access-date=6 November 2025}}</ref>

==Plot==
Sydney Brown, a well-dressed senior gambler, approaches John Finnegan, a homeless man in his mid-20s, sitting forlornly outside a diner in [[Sparks, Nevada]]. Sydney offers John a cigarette and buys him a cup of coffee. John tells Sydney that he went bust in Las Vegas and needs $6,000 for his mother's funeral. They travel to Vegas, where Sydney teaches John how to gamble in a casino with just $150 so that the casino will give him a free room and other complimentary amenities.

Two years later, John and Sydney are in Reno, where John has become Sydney's best friend and protégé. Calm and reserved, Sydney displays a fatherly care for John, who is unsophisticated. John has a new friend named Jimmy, who does security work, and is attracted to Clementine, a cocktail waitress in [[Reno, Nevada|Reno]]. Sydney meets Clementine and learns that she moonlights as a prostitute. Although Clementine believes Sydney might want to use her services, he wants to build a connection between John and her. Sydney asks John to show Clementine around town.

After receiving a frantic phone call, Sydney finds John and Clementine holding an unconscious tourist hostage in a nearby motel because he did not pay Clementine for sex. He learns that John and Clementine have called the hostage's wife, threatening to kill him if they do not get the money. After finding Jimmy's gun, Sydney convinces John and Clementine to flee the motel, advising them to leave town for a [[honeymoon]] as they have recently been impulsively married. While leaving, Sydney removes the evidence from the motel room.

Sydney meets with Jimmy, who tells him that the couple did not call the police. However, Jimmy explains that he has heard stories of Sydney killing John's father in [[Atlantic City, New Jersey|Atlantic City]]. Jimmy pulls a gun on Sydney and threatens to tell John unless Sydney gives him $10,000. Sydney says that he does not have it, but he can give $6,000 cash. They go to Sydney's suite and down to the casino floor, where Sydney gets the money from the cashier and gives it to Jimmy. John calls Sydney from a roadside phone to update him on the honeymoon. During the call, Sydney tells John that he loves him like a son. After hearing that, John thanks him and says that he also loves him. Jimmy takes the money to a casino and wins betting $2,000 on a hard eight. Sydney sneaks into Jimmy's house and when he returns, he kills him and takes his cash. The next day, Sydney returns to the diner where he met John and covers his bloodstained shirt cuff with a jacket sleeve.

==Production==
Originally titled ''Sydney'', it was [[Paul Thomas Anderson]]'s first feature film and the expansion of the short film ''[[Cigarettes & Coffee]]''.<ref name="sundancekids">{{cite book|url=https://archive.org/details/sundancekidshowm0000mott|url-access=registration|title=The Sundance Kids : how the mavericks took back Hollywood|last=Mottram|first=James|publisher=Faber & Faber, Inc|year=2006|isbn=9780865479678|location=NY|page=[https://archive.org/details/sundancekidshowm0000mott/page/129 129]}}</ref><ref name="rebels87">{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aQRM1yBVkjAC&q=rebels%20on%20the%20backlot&pg=PA87|title=Rebels on the backlot: six maverick directors and how they conquered the Hollywood studio system|last=Waxman|first=Sharon R.|publisher=[[HarperCollins]]|year=2005|isbn=978-0-06-054017-3|page=87}}</ref> The main character Sydney was named after Hall's previous role in ''[[Midnight Run]]''. Hall, Walters, Reilly, and Hoffman later starred in ''[[Boogie Nights]]'' and ''[[Magnolia (film)|Magnolia]]''.

Anderson said that he cast Hoffman in a supporting role after seeing him in ''[[Scent of a Woman (1992 film)|Scent of a Woman]]''.<ref>{{cite web|last=Brevet|first=Brad|title=Paul Thomas Anderson Remembers First Working with Philip Seymour Hoffman|date=April 14, 2014|website=Comingsoon.net|url=https://www.comingsoon.net/movies/news/590833-paul-thomas-anderson-remembers-first-working-philip-seymour-hoffman|accessdate=November 15, 2023}}</ref>  According to Hall, Hoffman improvised most of the dialogue his character says in his only scene in the film.<ref>{{cite magazine|last=Newman|first=Jason|title=Philip Baker Hall Remembers 'Genius' Philip Seymour Hoffman|date=February 3, 2014|magazine=Rolling Stone|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/tv-movies/tv-movie-news/philip-baker-hall-remembers-genius-philip-seymour-hoffman-176570/|accessdate=February 13, 2024}}</ref>

The film was influenced by and shares some plot elements with [[Jean-Pierre Melville]]'s 1956 film ''[[Bob le flambeur]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Eggert |first=Brian |date=2012-07-10 |title=Bob le flambeur |url=https://www.deepfocusreview.com/definitives/bob-le-flambeur/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170609184404/https://www.deepfocusreview.com/definitives/bob-le-flambeur/ |archive-date=2017-06-09 |access-date=2025-10-23 |website=Deep Focus Review}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Rivas |first=Andre |date=2011-11-21 |title=Review: Bob Le Flambeur (1956) |url=https://nextprojection.com/2011/11/21/review-bob-le-flambeur-1956/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111127141201/https://nextprojection.com/2011/11/21/review-bob-le-flambeur-1956/ |archive-date=2011-11-27 |access-date=2025-10-23 |website=Next Projection}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Ebert |first=Roger |author-link=Roger Ebert |date=2003-05-25 |title=Bob le Flambeur |url=https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-bob-le-flambeur-1955 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130429031641/https://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/great-movie-bob-le-flambeur-1955 |archive-date=2013-04-29 |access-date=2025-10-23 |website=[[RogerEbert.com]] |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lundegaard |first=Erik |date=2008-07-14 |title=Bob le flambeur (1956) |url=https://eriklundegaard.com/reviews/1956/foreign-france/bob-le-flambeur.php |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150907193320/https://eriklundegaard.com/reviews/1956/foreign-france/bob-le-flambeur.php |archive-date=2015-09-07 |access-date=2025-10-23 |website=eriklundegaard.com}}</ref>

In 2026, [[Nicolas Cage]] told ''[[The New York Times]]'' that he was offered a role in the film but he declined; he did not say which part he was offered.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/05/23/magazine/nicolas-cage-interview.html?unlocked_article_code=1.klA.SG7y.MgtXx2qYlKpI&smid=url-share|title=The Interview: Nicolas Cage Made Himself a Legend. Then He Had to Live With It.|publisher=The New York Times|last=Marchese|first=David|date=May 23, 2026|access-date=May 23, 2026|language=en}}</ref>

==Release and reception==
The film premiered in the American Spectrum section at the 1996 [[Sundance Film Festival]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://history.sundance.org/films/1375/sydney |title=Sydney / Archives / Sundance Institute |publisher=[[Sundance Institute]] |access-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-date=March 23, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160323014425/https://history.sundance.org/films/1375/sydney |url-status=live }}</ref> and then in the [[Un Certain Regard]] section at the [[1996 Cannes Film Festival]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/4724/year/1996.html |title=Festival de Cannes: Sydney |publisher=[[Cannes Film Festival]] |access-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-date=January 19, 2012 |url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120119014946/http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/4724/year/1996.html}}</ref> In 2018, Anderson said he was working on a Blu-ray release of the film.<ref>{{cite news |title=I'm Paul Thomas Anderson, writer and director of PHANTOM THREAD, AMA! |publisher=[[Reddit]] |work=IAmA |date=January 16, 2018 |url=https://www.reddit.com/r/IAmA/comments/7quthe/im_paul_thomas_anderson_writer_and_director_of/dss2rfb/ |last=Anderson |first=Paul Thomas |access-date=March 5, 2018 |archive-date=November 4, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211104214015/https://www.reddit.com/r/IAmA/comments/7quthe/im_paul_thomas_anderson_writer_and_director_of/dss2rfb/ |url-status=live }}</ref> An Australian Blu-ray for the film was released by Via Vision Entertainment in October 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Rosendorff|first=Kat|date=2021-08-24|title=Hard Eight (1996) - Standard Edition|url=https://viavision.com.au/shop/hard-eight-1996-standard-edition/|access-date=2021-11-25|website=Via Vision Entertainment|language=en-US}}</ref>

[[Roger Ebert]] gave the film three and a half stars out of four, writing "Movies like ''Hard Eight'' remind me of what original, compelling characters the movies can sometimes give us."<ref>{{cite news |title=Hard Eight |last=Ebert |first=Roger |date=February 27, 1997 |work=RogerEbert.com |publisher=Ebert Digital LLC |url=http://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/hard-eight-1997 |access-date=September 7, 2013 |archive-date=July 8, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130708173931/http://www.rogerebert.com/reviews/hard-eight-1997 |url-status=live }}</ref> [[Stephen Holden]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote "''Hard Eight'' is not a movie that wants to make a grand statement. It is really little more than a small resonant mood piece whose hard-bitten characters are difficult to like. But within its self-imposed limitations, it accomplishes most of what it sets out to do. And the acting is wonderfully understated, economical and unsentimental."<ref>{{cite news |title=Suspense-Filled Puzzle Draped in a Dark Mood |last=Holden |first=Stephen |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=February 28, 1997 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/02/28/movies/suspense-filled-puzzle-draped-in-a-dark-mood.html |access-date=April 11, 2018 |archive-date=April 12, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180412082230/https://www.nytimes.com/1997/02/28/movies/suspense-filled-puzzle-draped-in-a-dark-mood.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

On [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the film has an approval rating of 82% based on 89 reviews. The website's critical consensus reads, "An absorbing showcase for Philip Baker Hall, Paul Thomas Anderson's feature debut is a gamble that pays off handsomely."<ref>{{rotten-tomatoes|id=hard_eight|title=Hard Eight}}. {{Retrieved|access-date=May 20, 2025}}</ref> [[Metacritic]], which uses a [[Weighted arithmetic mean|weighted average]], assigned the film a score of 78 out of 100, based on 14 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.<ref name="Metacritic">{{cite web |title=''Hard Eight'' |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/hard-eight |website=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=[[Fandom (website)#Fandom, Inc.|Fandom, Inc.]] |access-date=September 22, 2025 |archive-url= |archive-date= |url-status=}}</ref> It is described by some authors as a [[neo-noir]] film.<ref>Conard, Mark T.; ed. (2009). ''The Philosophy of Neo-Noir''. Lexington: [[University Press of Kentucky]]. {{ISBN|081319217X}}.</ref>
